items.name: Education -- CONTROL r0
items.response:
Competing explanations of a sudden score jump are adjudicated not by weighing their intrinsic plausibility but by deriving from each a set of observable predictions and then asking which pattern the data actually display. The first task is to characterize the size of the gain and its distribution across classrooms, since the two accounts differ sharply on both. The district's average proficiency rate rose 20 percentage points in a single year. Gains concentrated in a small number of classrooms are a recognized signature of test administration irregularities. By contrast, a gain of two standard deviations in one year is typical of successful curriculum reforms. Which of these diagnostic profiles the district's results match is the point on which the dispute turns.

The next step is to assemble the documentary and statistical record for the year in question. The district adopted a new structured literacy curriculum in the same year as the score increase. Wrong-to-right erasure rates in several classrooms exceeded the state mean by more than four standard deviations. Even though the arrival of a new curriculum is precisely the chronology an innocent account requires, the concentration of gains in a handful of rooms remains the recognized marker of irregularity that it is. The answer-sheet evidence then admits of only two possibilities: either none of the district's schools had erasure rates flagged as statistically anomalous, or at least one of them did, and precisely one of these alternatives holds, never both. The erasure figures recorded for those classrooms show that the second alternative is the one that obtains.

Subsequent to that curricular adoption, researchers compared the district's gains with gains in demographically similar districts; that is, a difference-in-differences design was used to estimate the effect of the instructional reform. Difference-in-differences estimation requires no comparison group, and this cannot be squared with an estimator whose entire leverage comes from contrasting the district's trajectory with that of the matched districts just described. The inconsistency has to be resolved before any causal magnitude attributed to the reform can be taken at face value.

A further discriminating test is temporal: what happens to the measured gains once the tested cohort moves on. Instructional reforms generally produce gains that persist into the following school year. Score increases that vanish when students advance to a new grade indicate score inflation. Longitudinal follow-up of both the tested cohort and the classrooms themselves is thus the standard instrument for applying this criterion.

The last line of evidence is procedural rather than statistical. Investigators interviewed proctors and classroom teachers about testing-room procedures, and what those interviews yielded confirms that the state investigation documented chain-of-custody failures for answer sheets in multiple schools. Where the statistical anomalies, the failure of gains to persist, and the documented procedural lapses converge, the measured improvement is attributed to administration rather than to instruction; where they diverge, the reform account survives.
